$comment: Declared data dependencies. Rule: no consumer may depend on a field belonging to another index unless that dependency is declared here and checked. Coupling is not the problem — SILENT coupling is. The search.json -> counts -> empty-state relationship is legitimate and load-bearing; what was wrong with it was that nothing said so, and splitting the index would have broken a sentence in a UI with no test failing. checks.py asserts every declared field exists, and refuses a consumer that fetches an index it has not declared.

/api/search.json.counts.cities: printed by the empty state — this is the coupling point. If the index is ever split into search.json + counts.json, this line is what must force the consumer and its contract to be updated rather than silently falling back to a stale hard-coded number.

/api/atlas.json.cities: every destination it can route through
/api/atlas.json.journeys: the curated routes it compares against
/api/atlas.json.interests: matching a stated interest to a destination

/api/atlas.json.cities: resolving saved ids into places, and computing Travel DNA

/api/geo/europe-lod1.json.countries: the finer continent outline, fetched when zoom passes 1.6x
/api/geo/europe-lod1.json.nogeometry: the countries too small to draw at that scale

/api/geo/country/*.json.countries: one country's own level of detail, fetched when it is opened

published_only.$comment: Endpoints with no in-page consumer. They exist because the data is public and the documents are cheap. A shape change here breaks nobody inside this repository, which is exactly why the contract has to be written down: the consumers are people we cannot see.
